title: Cap. 6 Arg. 6: That easy human account of obtained grace is Pelagian—Rom. 9 and Phil. 2
pass_a_gloss: I now add: to give so obvious a reason on the human side of grace obtained or not obtained is the peculiar property of the Pelagians, and condemned by all the orthodox—who have always recalled the gift or denial of efficacious grace to the secret purpose of the divine good pleasure; nor did they think that, Christ's death having been granted, God is so bound to administer his grace promiscuously that having it or not having it would depend on the disparity of human wills. We do not deny the demerited unworthiness and voluntary wickedness of those who remain without grace, but we assert that all labor under this disease until they are cured by the remedy of special grace: and that none of the unregenerate draws grace to himself by a better will, but by a more efficacious grace given to him from the mere good pleasure of God receives a better will, according to that of the Apostle, "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy" (Romans 9:16). "It is God who gives us both to will and to accomplish according to his good will" (Philippians 2:13).
pass_b_english: I add this: to give so ready a reason, from the human side, why grace is obtained or missed is the Pelagian trademark—and every orthodox writer has condemned it. The orthodox have always traced the gift or denial of efficacious grace back to the secret purpose of God's good pleasure. They never held that, once Christ's death is granted, God is so bound to administer his grace indiscriminately that having it or lacking it turns on the disparity of human wills. We do not deny that those who stay without grace have earned their unworthiness and choose their wickedness. We do say that everyone labors under that disease until special grace cures it; and that no unregenerate person pulls grace to himself by a better will. Rather, by a more efficacious grace given from God's mere good pleasure, he receives a better will—as the Apostle says: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy" (Romans 9:16). "It is God who gives us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure" (Philippians 2:13).
source_text: Jam addo, ex parte hominis reddere tam obviam rationem gratiae obtentae aut non obtentae, est Pelagianorum proprium, & ab omnibus orthodoxis damnatum: qui gratiae efficacis donationem aut negationem ad arcanum propositum beneplaciti Divini semper revocarunt; neque putarunt, posita Christi morte, Deum ita teneri ad gratiam suam promiscue administrandam, ut eandem habere vel non habere ex disparitate humanarum voluntatum dependeret. Non negamus eorum demeritam indignitatem & improbitatem voluntariam, qui gratiae expertes manent, sed omnes hoc morbo laborare asserimus, donec specialis gratiae remedio curentur: nec irregenitorum quenquam per voluntatem meliorem trahere ad se gratiam, sed per gratiam efficaciorem ex mero Dei beneplacito illi donatam accipere voluntatem meliorem, juxta illud Apostoli, Non est volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei, Rom. ix. 16. Deus est qui dat nobis & velle & perficere pro bona sua voluntate, Phil. ii. 13.
